description_full: Cisco Systems, Inc. designs, develops, and sells technologies to power, help, secure, and draw insights from the internet in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, the Asia Pacific, Japan, and China. The company provides data center switching; network security, identity and access management, and secure access service edge; identity and agentic security solutions; interconnects public and private wireline and mobile networks, delivering connectivity to campus, data center, and branch networks; WEBEX suite, collaboration devices, and contact center; communication platform as a service software, including perpetual licenses, subscription arrangements, and hardware solutions; network assurance and observability suite; accelerated issue resolution, software support, and hardware replacement; professional services, such as planning, design, implementation, and high-value consulting; service and support packages, financing, and managed network services; and regional, national, and international wireline carriers, webscale products, internet, and cable. It also provides wireless products, including indoor and outdoor coverage designed for seamless roaming use of voice, video, and data applications; end-to-end collaboration solutions through cloud, on-premise, or within hybrid cloud environments. In addition, it offers technical support services. The company serves businesses, public institutions, governments, and service providers. It sells its products and services directly, through systems integrators, service providers, and resellers, and distributors. It has a collaboration with NVIDIA Corporation to develop Ultra-Dense Small Form Factor Pluggable (USFP), a high-density optical module pluggable transceiver. Cisco Systems, Inc. was incorporated in 1984 and is headquartered in San Jose, California.

Stock-based compensation of $46K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 12× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10). Recent headlines include layoff or workforce-reduction announcements.
financial_summary: Cisco Systems, Inc. is a mega-cap technology business with a $370.0B market cap on $63.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 9% cost of capital — a 15-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 63% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $12.8B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.07× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.5×.

Shareholder yield of 3.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Carries a 37% premium to sector median EV/EBITDA (confirmed by 1 other valuation measure)
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are net sellers (100% sell ratio, net $2.3M) — the people closest to the business are reducing their personal stake
Significant goodwill (46% of assets) from past acquisitions — a soft asset a conservative appraisal discounts to zero
Recent layoff news — often the market’s first signal that growth is under pressure or costs are being rebased
Technology sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 7% over 3 months
Elevated sector volatility (35% annualized) adds uncertainty
Cybersecurity liability and talent cost inflation — a single breach can erase years of goodwill, and the war for engineering talent compresses margins even at scale.

sector_tailwinds: Operating margins 17% above sector median — the quantitative trace of pricing power
Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
14 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 24% operating margin runs 17pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.04x).
It accounts for 1.4% of sector revenue and 1.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-13.5% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 68% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 21% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.86, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.8B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash, 36% in the 2022 bear market and 51% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $78.80 (margin of safety -19%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 36%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $56.28 to $113 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Technology peers: EV/EBITDA 21.1 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 111% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.5% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 25 covering analysts target $136 on average, 45% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 24% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 15pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It runs a 63% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow, or 14% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.07x.
ROE of 26% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 15.1% of revenue on R&D and 6.0% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.9x net debt to EBITDA ($14.3B of cash against $29.5B of debt), with interest covered 10.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.7, in the safe zone).
The current ratio of 0.93 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 46% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years, 4.9% over 5 years and 2.5% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 74% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 3%.
Capex runs 2.0x depreciation (2.2% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 83%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (11 sales, net $2.3M sold).
It returns 3.2% a year to shareholders (1.4% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 14 consecutive years, raising it 1.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 82,400 employees, each generates about $769K of revenue, 2.1x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 2.9% a year.
That works out to $155K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $9.5M (12x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
